text: This capstone follows one organization across three lessons: Meridian Trust Bank, a regional bank whose ServiceNow instance has four years of accumulated security debt, never fully reviewed since launch. You'll assess it, redesign it, and leave it with a real security review checklist — synthesizing everything from every earlier chapter of this course into one connected engagement.

Meridian runs ITSM, HR case management, and a few custom banking apps for 1,800 users across 40 branches. Roles, ACLs, and authentication settings have been added one request at a time by different admins, under deadline pressure, with nobody looking at the instance as a whole. That's not a hypothetical — it's the most common state a security architect actually walks into.

Finding one: role sprawl. Querying sys_user_role turns up 162 custom roles for 1,800 users — roughly one role per eleven people. Itil_l2_temp, itil_l2_temp_v2, and incident_approver_backup do nearly the same job, built by different admins with no shared contains_roles parent. The real cost isn't clutter — it's that quarterly access reviews become unreadable when one person holds nine overlapping roles.

Finding two: inconsistent field-level ACLs. The customer table's ssn field is gated by a scripted check against a purpose-built role. The comparably sensitive annual_income field on the same table has no script at all — just the generic itil role, held by over a thousand employees. Same sensitivity class, two completely unrelated levels of protection, because no consistent field-level design pattern was ever applied across the table.

Finding three: Meridian's broader IT organization standardized on Okta SSO with mandatory MFA three years ago — everywhere except ServiceNow, which was never migrated and still runs local accounts and passwords only. Finding four: neither sensitive field has its Audit flag enabled, so sys_audit holds zero history for either one. Paired with finding two's weak ACL, that's a sensitive field that's both under-protected and completely unmonitored.

Four named findings, each tied to a specific chapter and mechanism — not a vague sense that something's wrong. Lesson 23 takes each one and designs the actual fix: a redesigned role hierarchy, a real corrected ACL script, and a plan to move Meridian onto its own Okta standard.
